lessons.title: Subject and Object Markers — 이/가, 을/를
lessons.explanation: Korean uses particles (조사) attached to nouns to show their role. Subject markers: 이 (after consonant) / 가 (after vowel). Object markers: 을 (after consonant) / 를 (after vowel). The verb always goes at the END.
examples: 고양이가 물고기를 먹어요. (The cat eats fish.)
학생이 책을 읽어요. (The student reads a book.)
저가 한국어를 배워요. (I learn Korean.)
친구가 음악을 들어요. (My friend listens to music.)
lessons.tip: Choose 이/을 after a consonant, 가/를 after a vowel. Practice with common nouns until it's automatic.

quiz.question: Which subject marker comes after a vowel?
Where does the verb go in Korean?

lessons.title: Topic Marker — 은/는
lessons.explanation: 은/는 marks the topic of the sentence (what you're talking about). Use 은 after a consonant, 는 after a vowel. It often contrasts or emphasizes: 'As for X…' Korean is an SOV (Subject-Object-Verb) language.
examples: 저는 학생이에요. (As for me, I am a student.)
한국어는 어려워요. (As for Korean, it is difficult.)
커피는 좋아요. (As for coffee, I like it.)
오늘은 날씨가 좋아요. (As for today, the weather is good.)
lessons.tip: 은/는 often implies contrast: 나는 먹었어 (I ate) implies 'but someone else may not have'.

quiz.question: Which form of the topic marker comes after a consonant?

lessons.title: Polite Speech Level — -요 Ending
lessons.explanation: Korean has multiple speech levels. The most useful for beginners is the polite informal level, marked by -요 at the end of verbs and adjectives. It is appropriate for most daily conversations with adults who are not close friends.
examples: 먹어요 (I/you/he/she eats) — eats (polite)
공부해요 (I/you study) — studies (polite)
예뻐요 (It is pretty) — pretty (polite)
학교에 가요. (I go to school.) — polite
lessons.tip: The -요 ending is used for all persons and tenses in context — you can say 먹어요 and the context tells you who is eating.

quiz.question: What ending marks polite informal speech in Korean?

lessons.title: 이다 — To Be (Copula)
lessons.explanation: 이다 (to be) connects a subject to a noun predicate. Polite form: 이에요 (after consonant) / 예요 (after vowel). Formal: 입니다. Negative: 이/가 아니에요 (is not).
examples: 저는 학생이에요. (I am a student.)
이것은 책이에요. (This is a book.)
그것은 사과예요. (That is an apple.)
저는 선생님이 아니에요. (I am not a teacher.)
lessons.tip: 이다 is not a verb but a copula (connector). It attaches directly to the noun without a space.

quiz.question: How do you say 'This is a book' formally in Korean?

lessons.title: Location Particles — 에 and 에서
lessons.explanation: 에 marks static location (where something is/exists) or destination (where you're going). 에서 marks the location where an action takes place.
examples: 학교에 가요. (I go to school.) — destination
집에 있어요. (I am at home.) — static location
도서관에서 공부해요. (I study at the library.) — action location
학교에서 친구를 만났어요. (I met a friend at school.) — action location
lessons.tip: Key test: If the verb is 있다/없다 (exist) or a movement verb, use 에. If it's an action verb, use 에서.

quiz.question: Which particle marks where an action takes place?

lessons.title: Korean Adjectives (Descriptive Verbs)
lessons.explanation: Korean adjectives function grammatically like verbs — they conjugate for tense and speech level rather than needing a separate 'to be' verb. Adjective stems end in 다 in dictionary form, e.g., 예쁘다 (to be pretty), 크다 (to be big). Conjugation follows the same vowel harmony rules as verbs (아/어 endings).
examples: 이 꽃은 예뻐요. (This flower is pretty.)
날씨가 좋아요. (The weather is nice.)
그 가방은 커요. (That bag is big.)
오늘은 바빠요. (I am busy today.)
lessons.tip: Because adjectives conjugate like verbs, you never need a separate word for 'is/am/are' — just conjugate the adjective stem directly.

quiz.question: How do Korean adjectives behave grammatically?
What is the dictionary form ending for Korean adjectives?

lessons.title: Counters and Numbers — Native vs Sino-Korean
lessons.explanation: Korean has two number systems. Native Korean numbers (하나, 둘, 셋...) are used with counters for age, people (명/분), and objects (개). Sino-Korean numbers (일, 이, 삼...) are used for dates, money, phone numbers, and minutes. Choosing the right system is essential for correct counting.
examples: 사과 세 개 주세요. (Please give me three apples.) — native
저는 스물다섯 살이에요. (I am 25 years old.) — native
지금 두 시 삼십 분이에요. (It's 2:30 now.) — mixed: native hour, Sino minute
전화번호는 공일공입니다. (The phone number is 010...) — Sino
lessons.tip: Use native numbers for counting objects/age/hours, and Sino-Korean numbers for dates/money/minutes/phone numbers.

quiz.question: Which number system is used for telephone numbers?
Which counter word is used with native numbers for general objects?

lessons.title: Negation — 안 and 못
lessons.explanation: Korean has two main negation patterns. 안 (short form, placed before the verb) or -지 않다 (long form, attached to the verb stem) expresses simple negation ('not'). 못 (short form) or -지 못하다 (long form) expresses inability ('cannot'), due to circumstance rather than choice.
examples: 저는 커피를 안 마셔요. (I don't drink coffee.)
저는 커피를 마시지 않아요. (I don't drink coffee. — long form)
저는 수영을 못해요. (I can't swim.)
오늘은 바빠서 가지 못해요. (I can't go today because I'm busy.)
lessons.tip: 안 expresses a simple choice not to do something, while 못 expresses inability due to circumstances beyond your control.

quiz.question: Which negation word expresses inability rather than simple negation?
What is the long-form negation ending attached to a verb stem?

lessons.title: Connective Endings — -고, -(아/어)서, -(으)면
lessons.explanation: Korean connective endings join clauses. -고: 'and' (sequential or simultaneous). -(아/어)서: 'so' / 'because' / 'and then' (causal). -(으)면: 'if' / 'when' (conditional).
examples: 밥을 먹고 잠을 잤어요. (I ate and then slept.) — -고
비가 와서 집에 있었어요. (It rained so I stayed home.) — -(아/어)서
시간이 있으면 전화해요. (If you have time, call me.) — -(으)면
공부하고 놀아요. (I study and play.) — -고
lessons.tip: -(아/어)서 cannot be used with past tense before it — the tense marker goes on the final verb only.

quiz.question: Which ending expresses 'if/when' (conditional)?

lessons.title: Past Tense — -았/었-
lessons.explanation: Korean past tense is formed by inserting -았- or -었- before the sentence-final ending, chosen by vowel harmony: -았- follows stems with ㅏ/ㅗ vowels, -었- follows other vowels. 하다 verbs become 했-. The resulting form is then followed by -어요/-습니다 etc.
examples: 저는 어제 학교에 갔어요. (I went to school yesterday.)
밥을 먹었어요. (I ate rice/a meal.)
공부했어요. (I studied.)
날씨가 좋았어요. (The weather was good.)
lessons.tip: Check the last vowel of the verb stem — ㅏ or ㅗ takes 았, everything else takes 었, and 하다 always becomes 했.

quiz.question: Which past tense marker follows a stem ending in ㅏ or ㅗ?
What is the past tense stem of 하다 (to do)?

lessons.title: Future Tense and Intention — -겠-
lessons.explanation: -겠- is attached to a verb stem to express future action, intention, or strong conjecture/guess. It can mean 'will do,' 'plan to do,' or 'must be (the case)' depending on context. It is more assertive than the alternative future construction -(으)ㄹ 거예요.
examples: 제가 하겠습니다. (I will do it.)
내일 비가 오겠어요. (It looks like it will rain tomorrow. — conjecture)
먼저 가겠습니다. (I will go first.)
정말 힘들겠어요. (That must be really hard.)
lessons.tip: -겠- often shows determination or a confident guess, while -(으)ㄹ 거예요 is more neutral for simple future plans.

quiz.question: Besides future tense, what else can -겠- express?
Which sentence uses -겠- to express intention?

lessons.title: Passive Voice — 피동사
lessons.explanation: Korean passive verbs (피동사) are typically formed by inserting one of the infixes -이-, -히-, -리-, or -기- into the active verb stem. For many verbs without a direct passive form, -아/어지다 is attached instead to express a change of state or passive meaning.
examples: 문이 열려요. (The door opens/is opened.) — 열다 → 열리다
이 책은 많이 읽혀요. (This book is read a lot.) — 읽다 → 읽히다
창문이 닫혔어요. (The window was closed.) — 닫다 → 닫히다
날씨가 추워졌어요. (The weather became cold.) — 아/어지다 form
lessons.tip: There is no single rule for which infix (이/히/리/기) a verb takes — passive forms must be memorized individually.

quiz.question: Which infix pattern turns 열다 (to open) into its passive form?
What construction is used for verbs without a direct passive infix form?

lessons.title: Honorific Infixes and Speech Levels
lessons.explanation: Korean has elaborate honorific system. The infix -(으)시- is added to verbs to show respect for the SUBJECT. Vocabulary also changes: eat → 드시다 (honorific) vs. 먹다 (plain). Speech levels: formal polite (-습니다/-ㅂ니다), informal polite (-아/어요), plain (-아/어), informal (-아/어).
examples: 선생님이 가르치세요. (The teacher teaches.) — -(으)시-
할아버지가 드세요. (Grandfather is eating.) — honorific verb
어디 가세요? (Where are you going?) — polite + -(으)시-
사장님, 말씀해 주세요. (Please speak, director.)
lessons.tip: Use -(으)시- whenever you respect the subject — with teachers, elders, customers, and bosses.

quiz.question: What infix shows respect for the subject in Korean?

lessons.title: Causative Verbs — 사동사
lessons.explanation: Korean causative verbs (사동사) express making or letting someone do something. They are typically formed by inserting infixes -이-, -히-, -리-, -기-, -우-, -구-, or -추- into the verb stem, similar in form to passives but with causative meaning. Context and the resulting meaning distinguish them from passive forms.
examples: 엄마가 아이에게 밥을 먹였어요. (Mom fed the child. [made the child eat])
선생님이 학생을 웃겼어요. (The teacher made the student laugh.)
저는 동생을 울렸어요. (I made my younger sibling cry.)
문을 열었어요. (I opened the door.)
lessons.tip: Causative and passive infixes look similar (이/히/리/기), so you must learn each verb's causative form individually through exposure.

quiz.question: What does a Korean causative verb express?
options: an action done to the subject
making or letting someone do something

quiz.question: Which infix set is used to form Korean causative verbs?

lessons.title: Indirect/Reported Speech — -다고, -냐고, -라고, -자고
lessons.explanation: Korean reports what someone else said using quotative endings attached to the plain (diary) form of a verb: -다고 (statement), -냐고 (question), -라고 (command), -자고 (suggestion), typically followed by 하다 or 그랬다 ('said that'). These are commonly contracted in speech (-다고 해요 → -대요).
examples: 친구가 바쁘다고 했어요. (My friend said he/she was busy.) — statement
엄마가 어디 가냐고 물었어요. (Mom asked where I was going.) — question
선생님이 조용히 하라고 했어요. (The teacher told us to be quiet.) — command
같이 가자고 했어요. (He/she suggested going together.) — suggestion
lessons.tip: In casual speech, -다고 해요 often contracts to -대요, and -냐고 해요 to -냬요 — listen for these shortened forms.

quiz.question: Which quotative ending is used to report a command?
Which quotative ending reports a suggestion ('let's...')?

lessons.title: Speech Levels — 하십시오체 vs 해요체 vs 해체
lessons.explanation: Korean has multiple speech levels beyond basic politeness. 하십시오체 (formal polite, e.g., -습니다/-ㅂ니다) is used in news, presentations, and military/business settings. 해요체 (polite informal, -아/어요) is used in everyday polite conversation. 해체 (plain/casual, -아/어) is used with close friends and younger people.
examples: 안녕하십니까? (Hello — formal, 하십시오체)
안녕하세요? (Hello — polite, 해요체)
안녕? (Hi — casual, 해체)
이것을 확인해 주십시오. (Please confirm this. — formal business register)
lessons.tip: 하십시오체 sounds crisp and distant (news anchors, soldiers), while 해요체 is the safe default for daily life with people you don't know well.

quiz.question: Which speech level is typically used in news broadcasts and formal presentations?
Which speech level is appropriate for close friends?
